title: Is listing all permitted subclasses optional if they're in the same file?
shortTitle: Is listing all permitted subclasses optional if they're in the same file?
topicTitle: Is listing all permitted subclasses optional if they're in the same file?

s1_definition.profdef: Yes. If all of a sealed type's permitted direct subtypes are declared in the same source file (the same compilation unit) as the sealed type, the `permits` clause may be omitted. The compiler then infers the permitted set as exactly those subtypes declared in that file. This inference applies to auxiliary top-level classes in the file and to nested classes. If any permitted subtype lives in a different file, the `permits` clause becomes mandatory.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India writes its account-product policy on a single page. If every approved product is also fully described on that very same page, head office does not need to write a separate "approved list" at the top, because anyone reading the page can see the complete set of products right there. But if some approved products are described on other pages kept elsewhere, then head office must write an explicit "approved list" naming them, so readers know the full set without hunting through other documents. One page with everything needs no separate list; scattered pages do.
s1_definition.oneliner: The `permits` clause is optional only when all permitted subtypes are in the same source file, where the compiler infers them automatically.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes. If all of a sealed type's permitted direct subtypes are declared in the same source file (the same compilation unit) as the sealed type, the `permits` clause may be omitted. The compiler then infers the permitted set as exactly those subtypes declared in that file. This inference applies to auxiliary top-level classes in the file and to nested classes. If any permitted subtype lives in a different file, the `permits` clause becomes mandatory.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India writes its account-product policy on a single page. If every approved product is also fully described on that very same page, head office does not need to write a separate "approved list" at the top, because anyone reading the page can see the complete set of products right there. But if some approved products are described on other pages kept elsewhere, then head office must write an explicit "approved list" naming them, so readers know the full set without hunting through other documents. One page with everything needs no separate list; scattered pages do.

**One line to remember:** The `permits` clause is optional only when all permitted subtypes are in the same source file, where the compiler infers them automatically.

sections.s2_technical:
When you declare a type `sealed` you normally follow it with a `permits` clause naming the allowed direct subtypes. However, the Java language allows you to **omit `permits`** in one specific case: when every permitted direct subtype is declared in the **same source file** as the sealed type. In that situation the compiler scans the file and infers the permitted set to be exactly the subtypes declared there that directly extend or implement the sealed type.

This works because a single source file is a single compilation unit that the compiler reads in full, so it can see all the subtypes without needing an explicit list. The convenience is real for **small, closed hierarchies** written together. For example, a sealed interface `Shape` with record subtypes `Circle`, `Square`, and `Triangle` all in one file can skip the `permits` clause, and the compiler treats exactly those three as permitted. Adding a fourth subtype in the same file automatically extends the permitted set.

The inference covers both **auxiliary top-level classes** in the file and **nested** types. A single `.java` file may contain one public type and several package-private top-level types; if the sealed type and its subtypes are among these, inference works. It also works when the subtypes are nested inside the sealed type or alongside it. The key requirement is simply that they share the file.

The moment **any permitted subtype is in a different file**, the `permits` clause is **required**. You cannot mix inference and explicit listing: if even one subtype is outside the file, you must write the full `permits` clause naming every permitted direct subtype, including those that happen to be in the same file. So inference is an all-or-nothing convenience tied to co-location in one file.

A senior nuance is that relying on same-file inference couples the hierarchy to a single file, which is fine for small algebraic-data-type-style models but does not scale to large hierarchies that you naturally split across files for readability — there you write an explicit `permits`. Another nuance is that even with inference, each permitted subtype must still carry `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`, because that rule is independent of whether `permits` is written; records satisfy it implicitly by being final. A final nuance is that the inferred permitted set is still recorded in the `PermittedSubclasses` class-file attribute exactly as if you had written it, so at the bytecode level there is no difference — inference is purely a source-level convenience, and the sealing guarantee is identical.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India models a small, fixed set of transaction outcomes as a sealed hierarchy, and the whole model is small enough to live in one file. The bank wants to avoid the boilerplate of repeating the subtype names in a `permits` clause when the compiler can already see them in the same file. This is exactly same-file inference.

Problem 2 — As the model grows, one outcome type must move to its own file for reasons of size. The bank needs to understand that the moment a subtype leaves the file, the `permits` clause becomes mandatory and must name every direct subtype. We show both the inferred version and the explicit version.

Problem 3 — The bank wants to confirm that inference gives exactly the same sealing guarantee as an explicit list, so that an exhaustive switch still works. We demonstrate an exhaustive switch over the inferred sealed set.

In the mini-project we define, in one file, a sealed interface `TransactionResult` with record subtypes `Approved`, `Declined`, and `Pending`, omitting the `permits` clause, then a handler that switches exhaustively over them, logging each. Comments show the explicit `permits` version needed if a subtype moved to another file.

The code contains: a single-file sealed hierarchy using inference, record subtypes, a result handler, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transaction results — an approved transfer of 50,000, a declined transfer for insufficient funds, and a pending transfer awaiting OTP.

Step 1 — The compiler reads `SameFileDemo.java`. It sees the sealed interface `TransactionResult` with no `permits` clause, and it sees three record types in the same file that implement it. It infers the permitted set to be exactly `Approved`, `Declined`, and `Pending`.

Step 2 — `main` creates one instance of each result type. Each record is implicitly final, so it satisfies the rule that permitted subtypes must be final, sealed, or non-sealed, without any extra keyword.

Step 3 — For each result, `handler.describe(r)` runs a `switch` that pattern-matches the three record types. Because the sealed set is known and complete, the switch is exhaustive and needs no `default` branch. The compiler would reject the code if a case were missing.

Step 4 — The approved case logs the reference and amount, the declined case logs the reference and reason, and the pending case logs the reference and note. All three print, confirming that inference gives the same sealing and exhaustiveness guarantee as an explicit `permits` list.

```
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] APPROVED TXF-1 amount Rs.50000
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] DECLINED TXF-2 reason=Insufficient funds
2026-10-26 14:10:15 [INFO] PENDING  TXF-3 note=Awaiting OTP
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  SameFileDemo.java  (ONE compilation unit)
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ sealed interface TransactionResult   ← NO permits clause     │
  │   compiler scans THIS file and infers permitted set:        │
  │      { Approved, Declined, Pending }                        │
  │                                                             │
  │ record Approved(...)   implements TransactionResult (final) │
  │ record Declined(...)   implements TransactionResult (final) │
  │ record Pending(...)    implements TransactionResult (final) │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │ describe(r) → switch (exhaustive, no default)
        ▼
    Approved → "APPROVED TXF-1 amount Rs.50000"
    Declined → "DECLINED TXF-2 reason=Insufficient funds"
    Pending  → "PENDING  TXF-3 note=Awaiting OTP"

  If Pending moved to Pending.java → permits clause becomes REQUIRED.
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Same-File permits Inference ═══

  ┌─ Rules ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ all permitted subtypes in SAME FILE → permits optional        │
  │ any subtype in another file → permits REQUIRED (list all)     │
  │ records implicitly final → satisfy final/sealed/non-sealed    │
  │ inferred set recorded in PermittedSubclasses (same bytecode)  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ <<sealed interface>> TransactionResult    │  (no permits written)
  │ + reference(): String                     │
  └───────┬──────────┬───────────┬────────────┘
          │          │           │ inferred permitted set
          ▼          ▼           ▼
  ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐
  │Approved    │ │Declined    │ │Pending     │  (all records, final)
  │(ref,amount)│ │(ref,reason)│ │(ref,note)  │
  └────────────┘ └────────────┘ └────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ResultHandler                             │
  │ + describe(TransactionResult): String     │  exhaustive switch
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Call Chain:
    1. compiler infers {Approved, Declined, Pending}
    2. describe(Approved) → "APPROVED ..."
    3. describe(Declined) → "DECLINED ..."
    4. describe(Pending)  → "PENDING ..."
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, listing permitted subclasses is optional when all of them are declared in the same source file as the sealed type. In that case I can omit the permits clause entirely, and the compiler infers the permitted set to be exactly those subtypes declared in that file. This works because a single source file is one compilation unit the compiler reads in full, so it can already see the complete set without me repeating it.

This is a genuine convenience for small, closed hierarchies that I write together in one file, which is a common style for algebraic-data-type-style modelling. In my banking project I model transaction results as a sealed interface with three record subtypes, approved, declined, and pending, all in the same file, and I skip the permits clause. The compiler infers those three as the permitted set, and because records are implicitly final they automatically satisfy the rule that every permitted subtype must be final, sealed, or non-sealed.

The important boundary is that inference is all-or-nothing and tied to co-location. The moment any permitted subtype lives in a different file, the permits clause becomes mandatory, and then I must name every direct permitted subtype explicitly, including the ones still in the same file. So if my pending result grew large enough to move into its own file, I would have to add an explicit permits clause naming approved, declined, and pending. For large hierarchies I naturally split across files anyway, so I write permits explicitly there.

What I stress is that inference gives exactly the same guarantee as an explicit list. The inferred permitted set is recorded in the class file in the same PermittedSubclasses attribute, so at the bytecode level there is no difference, and the sealing is just as strong. That means my exhaustive switch over the result types still works with no default branch, and if a teammate adds a new result type in the file, every switch that is not exhaustive fails to compile. So same-file inference is purely a source-level convenience that removes boilerplate without weakening the closed-hierarchy safety a bank relies on.
